new_statements.quote: Word stress is a combination of the features of intensity, pitch and duration, which give a vowel prominence. It is distinct from the definitive accent, which always falls on the final vowel of a word (2.3.2, 4.7.2.1). Word stress is predictably placed according to a penultimate mora rule: The stress occurs on the vowel of the penultimate mora and on every second mora preceding. [...] [p.36] The most prominent syllable of a word is one containing a long vowel, or a rising diphthong. If neither of these is present, the primary stress falls on the penultimate mora.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is predictable and mora-counting: the penultimate mora of the word is stressed, with rhythmic stress on every second mora to its left; long vowels (VV) and rising diphthongs take stress as a unit on their first element (stress is shifted back onto the start of such a syllable, and no two successive morae may be stressed); each morpheme of a complex word is footed independently and monomoraic morphemes are unstressed. Within the word the most prominent (primary) stress is on a syllable with a long vowel (over a rising diphthong); absent either, primary stress is on the penultimate mora.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Alternating stress on every second mora preceding the penultimate mora; Salisbury notes levels are hard to rank because of phrase-stress overlay, that a long vowel outranks a rising diphthong, and that two long vowels/diphthongs in one word differ little (first marginally stronger) (pp.35-36).
new_statements.exceptions: 'Very few lexical exceptions': some common trisyllables have labile penult ~ initial stress (matua, atua, wawine, tangata, moana, wenua, punua, manava, puaka); some 4-6 syllable loans without compensatory lengthening violate the rule (patipika, komipiuta, polotatani, polokalamu, Palapalau); in CVCVCV words penult vs antepenult intensity differ little (small pitch rise); falling diphthongs /ia ua ie ue ea oa uo/ do not undergo stress redistribution; /iu, ui/ variable (pp.32-35).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rule, counted in morae from the right edge of the word, applied per morpheme in multi-morphemic words; bimoraic grammatical particles may bear stress. Explicitly distinguished from the NP-final 'definitive accent' (added final mora + pitch rise, sec. 2.3.2) and from pause/phrase stress (sec. 2.3.3). Supported by the author's duration measurements (Table 3, p.37).
new_statements.identity_note: Salisbury 2002 describes Pukapukan as spoken today on Pukapuka (Wale, Northern Cook Islands) and in the NZ/Australian diaspora communities; same languoid as Glottolog puka1242, no dialect split named.

sources.locator: Ch.2 Phonology, sec. 2.3.1 'Word Stress', printed p.31 (PDF p.53); primary-stress sentence printed p.36 (PDF p.58); exceptions p.34-35
sources.note: Ch.2 sec. 2.3.1 Word Stress (pp.31-36): stress predictable by a penultimate-mora rule with alternating stress on every second mora leftward; long vowels/rising diphthongs take stress as a unit (stress redistribution), no stress on successive morae, each morpheme parsed independently; primary stress = syllable with long vowel or rising diphthong, else penultimate mora; a handful of labile 3-syllable words and some loans are exceptions; distinct from the phrase-final 'definitive accent' (2.3.2) and phrase stress (2.3.3). Includes duration measurements (Table 3).
Phonology section lists consonants/vowels only, nothing on stress; bibliography supplied the open link to Salisbury 2002 (pukapuka.world / Wayback).
